name: growth beats hardware
hook: Two correct functions. One finishes in a blink, the other takes days. A faster computer won't save it.
hook_slide: Same answer. One takes a blink. The other takes *days*.
hook_sub: And a faster computer won't save it.
caption: Two functions that both decide whether any two numbers sum to a target. Both correct. On {n1} numbers one makes {checks_a} pair checks, the other {checks_b} set lookups.
At about 10⁸ simple operations a second, {big} numbers cost about {a_seconds} seconds against {b_ms} millisecond. At {huge}: about {a_days} days against {b_seconds} seconds.
So buy a machine {speedup}× faster? A linear algorithm handles {speedup}× more data. A quadratic one, {quad_gain}×. An exponential one, about {exp_gain} more elements.
The shape of the growth curve is a property of your algorithm, and no amount of hardware budges it.
What's the worst accidental O(n²) you've shipped? 👇
cta: Start here: it is the first lesson of the Big O module.

rows.lab: Version B: remember what you saw

p: Nothing about correctness distinguishes them. Only their growth does.
Version A didn't just get a little slower. It fell off a cliff.

slides.h: The curve belongs to the algorithm
p: The shape of the growth curve is a property of your algorithm, and no amount of hardware budges it.
That is why we count operations, not seconds.
